newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany's IG Metall lays out 97 pay strategy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany's IG Metall lays out 97 pay strategy.

text.p: Germany's largest engineering union, the powerful IG Metall, on Tuesday laid out its pay demand for 1997, putting a clear emphasis on job security as a major goal of this year's pay negotiations.
The union's chairman Klaus Zwickel said after a meeting of IG Metall's management board the union's leaders recommended a pay claim of between 4.5 and five percent for next year.

But he also made clear that this did not mean the union was determined to achieve a pay rise running at more than double the expected inflation rate. Rather, the workers wanted a combination deal which would also secure jobs, he said.

"We have been put under pressure by dramatic erroneous developments in employment policies," Zwickel told a news conference. "Job security will have the highest priority for IG Metall in the 1997 wage round."

The total wage demand of 4.5 to five percent was made up of two components, a 2.5 to three percent compensation for increased productivity and two percent for expected inflation, Zwickel told reporters.

"The productivity component of 2-1/2 to three percent, should be used exclusively for goals related to job security policies," he said, adding that the union's aim in terms of basic pay would be to secure real spending power.

Zwickel earlier this year proposed a broad "Alliance for Jobs" aimed at securing and creating employment which fell through after the government, unions and employers failed to find common ground in terms of possible measures.
Yet within the engineering sector, the union itself is ironically seen as being largely to blame for the persistently high level of lay-offs and unemployment.

IG Metall some 18 months ago secured a pay deal for its members which was hailed as a huge victory for the unions, offering workers a 3.4 percent rise in May 1995 and a further 3.6 percent increase in November of that year.

That high pay increase backfired on the union to some extent. Independent economists with hindsight blame that pay deal and others in the 1995 payround for helping to tip the German economy into a downturn late last year.
The 1997 pay claim comes at a time when the union is already at loggerheads with employers over new legislation allowing companies to cut sick pay to 80 percent of the normal wage from 100 percent.
The union reached an uneasy truce with the employers' association on Monday after vast walk-outs last week made companies realise the union would not simply acquiesce to the reduction in benefits.
The employers agreed to urge companies to reverse decisions to implement the sick pay cut immediately in return for a pledge from the union to drop its protest campaign.

Zwickel, who will hold more talks with the employers on the sick pay issue on Thursday, said it was unclear at the moment whether the dispute over benefit cuts would be merged into the 1997 pay negotiations.
He accepted that the union side might have to make certain concessions, but made no comment on what these could be.
"It is too early to say at the moment how we will get to an overall solution on this," he said. "At the moment I must warn against false hopes."

With today's announcement of the board's recommendation, responsibility for the pay negotiations passes to the unions' regional negotiators, who then make a concrete demand in line with the board's recommendation.
But Zwickel said it could not be excluded that the union's regional leaders would choose to put the sick pay cuts on the agenda at those talks as well.
It was still "completely open" in which direction these discussions might go, he said.
